title: Programming
coreMove: Force a technical skill into a runnable slice where output, error, and debugging can teach the next move.
sourcePressure: The source frames programming as a cognitively dense domain where breakdown, real-problem iteration, and avoidance of endless research matter more than abstract study hoarding.
chapterSpecificMisunderstanding: Treating programming as either pure concept study or random hacking, instead of a small build-test-fix loop on a real problem.

sourceAnchors.name: programming
sourceAnchors.detail: the frozen support names programming as the case chapter and frames it through breakdown, real-problem iteration, and avoiding endless research
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: Programming starts teaching when the idea becomes a small thing that runs, breaks, and points to the next fix.

sourceAnchors.name: real-problem iteration
sourceAnchors.detail: the source says real working problems teach more than endless abstract study in this chapter
sourceAnchors.phrasingHint: A real problem gives the lesson teeth because the code either changes the output or it does not.

exampleOpeningDiversity.rule: no more than 2 of the 6 examples may open with the pattern 'At HH:MM, <Name> <verb>s'
exampleOpeningDiversity.requiredOpenings: at least 4 distinct opening devices across the 6 examples, drawn from: timestamp+name+action, dialogue first line, sensory detail first, second-person You direct address, retrospective It took her three weeks to see, question-as-hook, environmental detail before any human
exampleOpeningDiversity.rationale: C8 catches Cartesian repetition of phrases but not the deeper template of 'timestamp + named protagonist + prop + decision' that makes 6 examples feel like 1 example with name swaps

rhythmVariety.deepReadParagraphLengthMix: at least one paragraph 3 sentences or shorter, at least one paragraph 5+ sentences, at least one one-sentence punch line
rhythmVariety.fullReadInterludeRequirement: at least one paragraph that breaks the scene-then-rule rhythm - a question to the reader, a research aside, a direct second-person passage, or a brief historical reference
rhythmVariety.forbiddenRhythm: every paragraph following the pattern 'concrete anchor sentence -> abstract rule sentence -> elaboration sentence'

exampleSpecs.audience: a workplace learner with one repetitive technical problem
exampleSpecs.stakes: expired stock counts are being copied by hand every Friday
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Thomas reduces the project to one script that flags dates older than today, runs it on a copied sheet, reads the first error, and fixes only that input format
exampleSpecs.firstImage: orange expiry stickers stacked beside a duplicated inventory sheet

exampleSpecs.audience: a research assistant who keeps reading libraries instead of testing data
exampleSpecs.stakes: a grant report depends on removing impossible temperature readings
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ingrid sees that progress began when she stopped comparing libraries and wrote a tiny filter against ten ugly sensor rows
exampleSpecs.firstImage: ten sensor rows printed with one impossible minus sign circled

exampleSpecs.audience: a volunteer solving a real event problem under a deadline
exampleSpecs.stakes: opening night check-in fails if the ticket list cannot load
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: David asks what one field must import first, writes the smallest parser for seat number, and lets the rejected comma line reveal the next bug
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a box-office laptop balanced on a stack of playbills

exampleSpecs.domain: wildlife rescue volunteer building a feeding-reminder SMS rule
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who needs code tied to a visible service result
exampleSpecs.stakes: orphaned animals miss interval checks when paper notes get buried
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Paula chooses one reminder rule for one enclosure, sends a test message to herself, and debugs the wrong time zone before adding any other feature
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a laminated feeding chart clipped to a wire enclosure door

exampleSpecs.audience: a learner turning curiosity into one executable tool
exampleSpecs.stakes: reporters waste hours because scanned article dates sort incorrectly
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Ben predicts more regex reading will solve it, then learns faster by running one date-normalizer against twelve bad archive filenames
exampleSpecs.firstImage: twelve scanned filenames glowing in a narrow search pane

exampleSpecs.domain: airport baggage desk macro for damage-form IDs
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader whose technical problem is small but costly
exampleSpecs.stakes: duplicate claim IDs create angry passenger calls by noon
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: Kiran stops studying macro syntax broadly, builds one ID-check function, runs it on yesterday's forms, and fixes the one duplicate case it misses
exampleSpecs.firstImage: a torn suitcase handle resting beside a stack of damage forms

skillTargets: choose runnable slices over abstract technical sprawl
use errors as feedback without glamorizing failure
detect research hoarding in programming practice
map breakdown to a real output and next debug step

tryThisNowSpec: Write the smallest technical output your current learning project could produce today, plus the first thing that could fail when you run it.
